arXiv:2505.00586v1 [cs.RO] 01 May 2025

ParkDiffusion: Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Multi-Modal Trajectory Prediction for Automated Parking using Diffusion Models

Jiarong Wei Affiliation:  CARIAD SE, Germany. Affiliation:  Department of Computer Science, University of Freiburg, Germany.    Niclas Vödisch Affiliation:  Department of Computer Science, University of Freiburg, Germany.    Anna Rehr Affiliation:  CARIAD SE, Germany.    Christian Feist Affiliation:  CARIAD SE, Germany.    Abhinav Valada Affiliation:  Department of Computer Science, University of Freiburg, Germany.
Abstract

Automated parking is a critical feature of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS), where accurate trajectory prediction is essential to bridge perception and planning modules. Despite its significance, research in this domain remains relatively limited, with most existing studies concentrating on single-modal trajectory prediction of vehicles. In this work, we propose ParkDiffusion, a novel approach that predicts the trajectories of both vehicles and pedestrians in automated parking scenarios. ParkDiffusion employs diffusion models to capture the inherent uncertainty and multi-modality of future trajectories, incorporating several key innovations. First, we propose a dual map encoder that processes soft semantic cues and hard geometric constraints using a two-step cross-attention mechanism. Second, we introduce an adaptive agent type embedding module, which dynamically conditions the prediction process on the distinct characteristics of vehicles and pedestrians. Third, to ensure kinematic feasibility, our model outputs control signals that are subsequently used within a kinematic framework to generate physically feasible trajectories. We evaluate ParkDiffusion on the Dragon Lake Parking (DLP) dataset and the Intersections Drone (inD) dataset. Our work establishes a new baseline for heterogeneous trajectory prediction in parking scenarios, outperforming existing methods by a considerable margin.

I Introduction

Automated parking has emerged as a prominent driver assistance system, driven by the increasing demand for convenience, safety, and space efficiency in urban environments. A critical component is trajectory prediction, which bridges the perception and planning modules and, hence, directly impacts the overall performance. Nonetheless, most existing studies in automated parking discuss aspects such as perception [1, 2], localization [3, 4], and planning [5, 6]. Consequently, the vast majority of work toward trajectory prediction focuses on generic urban traffic [7, 8, 9, 10] or pedestrian-only scenarios [11, 12, 13] rather than the challenges that occur in parking environments.

Unlike typical roadways, parking lots are often less structured and have fewer traffic regulations, as illustrated in Fig. 1. They frequently lack defined opposing lanes, and vehicles may travel against one-way directions. Moreover, road user behavior is usually less predictable, with vehicles making abrupt turns into unoccupied parking spaces or reversing without adequate visibility. Finally, both vehicles and vulnerable road users (VRUs), such as pedestrians, often share the same space without dedicated sidewalks or pedestrian crossings. Although the driving speed in parking lots is typically lower than on standard roads, these challenges increase the risk of unsafe interactions.

In this work, we address trajectory prediction in the context of automated parking. Specifically, we propose the novel ParkDiffusion model, which addresses the following key aspects: (1) the varying behavior of heterogeneous road users, such as passenger cars and pedestrians; (2) multi-agent forecasting, enabling the simultaneous prediction of future trajectories for multiple road users while accounting for their interactions; and (3) multi-modal trajectories, facilitating the integration of probabilistic-driven approaches.

The objective of our work is to predict future trajectories of road users in parking scenarios, given their previous positions and additional contextual information. We build ParkDiffusion on the concept of diffusion [11] due to its capability of modeling complex probabilistic distributions. We propose a novel dual map encoder that separately processes soft traffic regulations such as lane markings and hard obstacles such as parked cars. We further include an agent type embedding to account for heterogeneous road users. Finally, we combine learning-based modules with a physics-driven approach that models the kinematics of different agent types.

To summarize, the main contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We introduce ParkDiffusion, a novel method for multi-agent and multi-modal trajectory prediction in challenging parking scenarios.

  2. 2.

    We present the first work on heterogeneous trajectory prediction that explicitly considers VRUs in parking scenarios, enhancing the safety of automated parking.

  3. 3.

    We integrate physics-based kinematic constraints to generate more realistic and feasible trajectories.

  4. 4.

    We perform extensive experiments on the DLP [14] and inD [15] datasets which demonstrate that ParkDiffusion achieves state-of-the-art performance.

II Related Work

We present an overview of trajectory prediction, diffusion models for this task, and relevant works on automated parking.

Trajectory Prediction: The task of trajectory prediction focuses on forecasting an agent’s motion based on past trajectories. Related works evolve from traditional methods, such as the Extended Kalman Filter, to learning-based methods that offer a more comprehensive understanding of the environment. SceneTransformer [16] jointly predicts all agents’ behaviors, yielding consistent futures that account for their interactions. MultiPath++ [17] proposes a context-aware fusion of these elements and develops a multi-context gating fusion component for better feature representation. QCNet [7] introduces a query-centric paradigm for scene encoding, reusing past computations to improve prediction efficiency. SIMPL [8] proposes a global fusion module with symmetric directed message passing, enabling single-pass forecasting for all road users.

An important variation of the vanilla tasks is trajectory prediction for heterogeneous agents, which facilitates an advanced understanding of the scene by forecasting trajectories for various agent types, such as vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians. Some methods utilize scene graph-structured models  [18, 19] to represent interactions among road users, incorporating both agent-to-agent and agent-to-environment interactions. Another common approach is based on long short-term memory networks (LSTMs). TraPHic [20] models inter-agent interactions with an LSTM-CNN hybrid network. TrafficPredict [21] refines heterogeneous predictions using instance and category layers with an LSTM. In contrast to standard LSTM designs, Li et al. [22] employ hierarchical convolutional networks and multi-task learning to predict the trajectories of heterogeneous road agents. Other lines of work employ attention-based approaches. For instance, Zhao et al. [23] propose a dual attention model that captures interactions between road users and their impact on future trajectories. In our work, we account for heterogeneous agents by using an agent type embedding module and by explicitly modeling the different kinematics of cars and vulnerable road users (VRUs) such as pedestrians. In parking scenarios, cars and pedestrians often share the same space, thereby increasing the risk of unsafe interactions and highlighting the need for type-specific considerations.

Diffusion Models for Trajectory Prediction: Diffusion-based generative models have emerged as powerful tools for capturing the inherent uncertainty and multi-modality of future motion. Recent studies explore diffusion models from various perspectives. Liu et al. [24] decouple prediction uncertainty into intention and action components to enhance diffusion models’ capacity. MotionDiffuser [25] learns a joint multi-modal distribution for multi-agent trajectory prediction. Li et al. [26] employ a coarse-to-fine approach, generating trajectory proposals using a conditional variational autoencoder, followed by refinement through a conditional diffusion model. Lv et al. [27] propose an autoencoder diffusion model of pedestrian group relationships for multi-modal trajectory prediction. Choi et al. [28] use diffusion models for efficient future trajectory prediction through an optimized sampling mechanism. ControlTraj [29] integrates road network constraints to guide the geographical outcomes. BCDiff [30] predicts trajectories from instantaneous observations to address limited observation time.

One key drawback of diffusion models is their difficulty in real-time applications due to the large number of denoising steps required. To overcome this challenge, we leverage the Leapfrog Diffusion (LED) framework [11], which enhances the diffusion model efficiency by introducing an LED Initializer that skips a large number of denoising steps. Although our approach is based on the Leapfrog skeleton, we introduce several key innovations, including the dual map encoder, agent type embedding, and kinematic refinement, as outlined in our list of contributions, resulting in significant performance improvements in both vehicles and pedestrians over the vanilla LED model. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to utilize diffusion models for heterogeneous trajectory prediction in complex parking scenarios.

Automated Parking: Automated parking is a key component of driver assistance systems, driven by demand for enhanced comfort, safety, and spatial efficiency in dense urban areas. Owing to challenges distinct from general urban driving, research on automated parking has examined components such as perception [1, 2], planning [5, 6], localization [3, 4], SLAM [31, 32], or combinations of these components [33, 34]. Nonetheless, despite posing a vital link between perception and planning, the task of trajectory prediction remains understudied. Existing relevant works include ParkPredict [35] and ParkPredict++ [14]. ParkPredict compares LSTM-based models with an Extended Kalman Filter, underscoring intent’s impact on future trajectories. ParkPredict++ extends this by leveraging convolutional and transformer-based architectures to extract spatiotemporal features from trajectory histories and bird’s-eye-view semantic maps. However, both works adopt a sequential learning paradigm in which parking intent is inferred first, followed by the forecasting of future trajectories. Additionally, these methods are limited to single-modal and vehicle-only trajectory prediction with low accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, our work represents the first step toward trajectory prediction for multiple heterogeneous road users tailored for automated parking.

III Method

In this section, we introduce our ParkDiffusion approach for heterogeneous multi-agent multi-modal trajectory prediction, as depicted in Fig. 2. Following a formal definition of the research problem, we outline the key components, which include: (1) an ego vehicle-centric data preprocessing pipeline; (2) an agent encoder that combines a transformer encoder with a spatiotemporal encoder; (3) a dual map encoder that separately processes soft and hard map constraints, followed by an attention-based feature fusion mechanism; (4) an agent type embedding module to facilitate agent-specific feature representation; and (5) a kinematic refinement module to generate more physically feasible trajectories. We also introduce the denoiser and the training procedure of our method.

III-A Problem Formulation

The primary objective of our work is to predict future trajectories of all road users within the perception range of the ego vehicle, given their previous positions and additional context information. We denote the set of all agents as 𝒜={a𝑒𝑔𝑜,a1,a2,…,aN}\mathcal{A}=\{a_{\mathit{ego}},a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{N}\}, comprising the ego vehicle a𝑒𝑔𝑜a_{\mathit{ego}} and other road users including cars and pedestrians. Each agent a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} is observed for TpT_{p} past timestamps, and its motion is predicted for TfT_{f} future timestamps. Let Xa=[xa−Tp+1,xa−Tp+2,…,xa0]∈ℝTp×2X_{a}=[x_{a}^{-T_{p}+1},x_{a}^{-T_{p}+2},\dots,x_{a}^{0}]\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{p}\times 2} denote the past trajectories of agent aa. Collectively, we have X𝒜={Xa𝑒𝑔𝑜,Xa1,Xa2,…,XaN}X_{\mathcal{A}}=\{X_{a_{\mathit{ego}}},X_{a_{1}},X_{a_{2}},\dots,X_{a_{N}}\}. The context is given by a map representation MM consisting of map polylines and static obstacle polylines. Our goal is to predict for each agent a sequence of future positions Ya=[ya1,ya2,…,yaTf]∈ℝTf×2Y_{a}=[y_{a}^{1},y_{a}^{2},\dots,y_{a}^{T_{f}}]\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{f}\times 2}. The multi-modal nature of the prediction is captured by defining 𝒴a={Ya1,…,YaK}\mathcal{Y}_{a}=\{Y_{a}^{1},\dots,Y_{a}^{K}\} to yield KK plausible trajectories, where Yak∈𝒴aY_{a}^{k}\in\mathcal{Y}_{a} represents the kt​hk^{th} candidate trajectory of agent aa.

We define our model as ℳθ​(⋅)\mathcal{M}_{\theta}(\cdot) with parameter θ\theta such that:

ℳθ​(X𝒜,M)=Pθ​(𝒴𝒜∣X𝒜,M)\mathcal{M}_{\theta}(X_{\mathcal{A}},M)=P_{\theta}(\mathcal{Y}_{\mathcal{A}}\mid X_{\mathcal{A}},M) (1)

PθP_{\theta} represents the conditional probability distribution over the future trajectories 𝒴𝒜\mathcal{Y}_{\mathcal{A}} given the past observations X𝒜X_{\mathcal{A}} and the map context MM. The overall learning problem is:

θ∗=arg​minθ∑a∈𝒜mink∈{1,…,K}ℒ(Yak,Ya),\theta^{*}=\argmin_{\theta}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\min_{k\in\{1,\dots,K\}}\mathcal{L}\left(Y_{a}^{k},Y_{a}\right)\,, (2)

where ℒ\mathcal{L} measures the discrepancy between predicted trajectories and the ground truth to minimize the best-match error.

III-B Data Preprocessing

We first preprocess the data into ego vehicle-centric samples. For each sample, we collect all agent and context information within a 20 m20\text{\,}\mathrm{m} radius of the ego vehicle and transform all relevant information into the ego vehicle coordinate system. The state of each agent is represented as a 12-dimensional feature vector in the ego vehicle coordinate system: (x,y,h,v,ax,ay,xrel,yrel,hrel,vrel,axrel,ayrel)(x,y,h,v,a_{x},a_{y},x^{\textit{rel}},y^{\textit{rel}},h^{\textit{rel}},v^{\textit{rel}},a_{x}^{\textit{rel}},a_{y}^{\textit{rel}}), where xx and yy denote the coordinates, hh represents the heading angle, vv is the velocity, axa_{x} and aya_{y} correspond to the acceleration components along the xx and yy axes, and the quantities with the superscript rel are computed relative to the ego vehicle. Importantly, the velocity of each agent is computed as a signed quantity, which is crucial in the context of automated parking with frequent reverse maneuvers.

III-C Encoding

In this section, we introduce the key components for encoding, including the agent encoder, dual map encoder, agent type embedding, and kinematic refinement.

Agent Encoder: The agent encoder aims to capture the spatiotemporal features of the past trajectories of each agent. This module comprises two complementary steps. First, the agent history is processed via a linear projection followed by two transformer encoder layers with self-attention, yielding refined features with a residual connection. Additionally, a spatiotemporal encoder employs a convolution layer to extract local spatial patterns from the trajectory data, and a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) aggregates these features temporally to produce a feature embedding. The resulting agent features are then concatenated to serve as the basis for subsequent context fusion with map and agent type information in our diffusion framework, denoted by 𝐞a\mathbf{e}_{a}.

Dual Map Encoder: To robustly capture the environmental context, we design a dual map encoder that separately processes map information and static objects, both represented as polylines. While map data provides soft constraints (e.g., lane markings that could be crossed), static objects pose hard constraints (e.g., vehicles parked in parking spots that need to be avoided). We denote the corresponding sets of soft and hard polylines as 𝒫soft={p1,p2,…,pNsoft}\mathcal{P}_{\text{soft}}=\{p_{1},p_{2},\dots,p_{N_{\text{soft}}}\} and 𝒫hard={q1,q2,…,qNhard}\mathcal{P}_{\text{hard}}=\{q_{1},q_{2},\dots,q_{N_{\text{hard}}}\}, respectively.

Our dual map encoder consists of two parallel branches. The soft branch processes 𝒫soft\mathcal{P}_{\text{soft}} using a two-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to generate map feature embeddings 𝐟soft\mathbf{f}_{\text{soft}} that capture high-level map semantic features. Similarly, the hard branch processes 𝒫hard\mathcal{P}_{\text{hard}} via a separate two-layer MLP to produce features 𝐟hard\mathbf{f}_{\text{hard}} that emphasize geometric constraints. After encoding, both sets of polyline features are fused using a two-step cross-attention mechanism. First, the agent features are refined by attending to the soft polyline features:

𝐞a,soft=softmax⁡(𝐞a​𝐟soft⊤d)​𝐟soft,\mathbf{e}_{a,\text{soft}}=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{e}_{a}\,\mathbf{f}_{\text{soft}}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)\mathbf{f}_{\text{soft}}\,, (3)

where 𝐞a\mathbf{e}_{a} denotes the agent feature, dd denotes the feature dimension, and 𝐟soft\mathbf{f}_{\text{soft}} is the collection of soft constraints embeddings. Next, the refined agent feature further attends to the hard polyline features:

𝐞a,map=𝐞a,soft+softmax⁡(𝐞a,soft​𝐟hard⊤d)​𝐟hard,\mathbf{e}_{a,\text{map}}=\mathbf{e}_{a,\text{soft}}+\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\mathbf{e}_{a,\text{soft}}\,\mathbf{f}_{\text{hard}}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}\right)\mathbf{f}_{\text{hard}}\,, (4)

with 𝐟hard\mathbf{f}_{\text{hard}} denoting the collection of hard embeddings. This residual connection integrates both sources of contextual information, yielding a map-conditioned agent representation.

Agent Type Embedding: To account for heterogeneous agents, we employ an agent type embedding mechanism that modulates the map-conditioned agent features 𝐞a,map\mathbf{e}_{a,\text{map}} based on their type. Each agent is associated with a type label, such as vehicle or pedestrian. Rather than using a simple lookup, the agent type information is first mapped to a learnable embedding and then processed through an MLP layer to generate modulation parameters γ\gamma and β\beta. For each agent, the combined feature 𝐟c\mathbf{f}_{c} is modulated as follows:

𝐟c=𝐞a,map⋅(1+γ)+β,\mathbf{f}_{c}=\mathbf{e}_{a,\text{map}}\cdot(1+\gamma)+\beta\,, (5)

where the element-wise multiplication scales the features and the addition of β\beta shifts them. This adaptive modulation enables the network to dynamically condition the agent features on their type, thereby improving the downstream trajectory prediction performance.

III-D Kinematic Refinement

A potential problem with black-box models for motion forecasting is that model outputs can be physically infeasible or lack the general characteristics of natural motion [36] [37]. To address this problem, we employ kinematic constraint layers for both vehicles and pedestrians, bridging the transformation from control signals to the refined trajectories. For any agent aa, the position at timestamp tt is defined as:

𝐩a​(t)=(pa,x​(t),pa,y​(t)),\mathbf{p}_{a}(t)=(p_{a,x}(t),\,p_{a,y}(t))\,, (6)

the velocity as:

𝐯a​(t)=(va,x​(t),va,y​(t)),\mathbf{v}_{a}(t)=(v_{a,x}(t),\,v_{a,y}(t))\,, (7)

and the control input as:

𝐮a​(t)=(ua,x​(t),ua,y​(t)).\mathbf{u}_{a}(t)=(u_{a,x}(t),\,u_{a,y}(t)). (8)

Note that 𝐮a​(t)\mathbf{u}_{a}(t) is the output of the Leapfrog Diffusion Initializer [11], as shown in Fig. 2, which takes the combined feature 𝐟c\mathbf{f}_{c} of the agent type embedding module as input. We also attach a probability branch (a simple MLP layer that takes the combined feature 𝐟c\mathbf{f}_{c} as input and outputs probabilities) inside the Initializer to learn the probabilities of the multi-modal trajectory predictions. For further details on the LED Initializer, please refer to the work by Mao et al. [11].

Vehicle Kinematics: The state of vehicles is defined as:

𝐳a​(t)=(𝐩a​(t),𝐯a​(t)),\mathbf{z}_{a}(t)=(\mathbf{p}_{a}(t),\,\mathbf{v}_{a}(t))\,, (9)

The kinematics are modeled via a point-mass system with acceleration control inputs. The state evolves according to:

𝐩˙a​(t)=𝐯a​(t),𝐯˙a​(t)=𝐮a​(t).\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{a}(t)=\mathbf{v}_{a}(t),\quad\dot{\mathbf{v}}_{a}(t)=\mathbf{u}_{a}(t)\,. (10)

The control input is constrained by

‖𝐮a​(t)‖≤μ​g,\|\mathbf{u}_{a}(t)\|\leq\mu g\,, (11)

where μ=0.7\mu=0.7 is the road adhesion coefficient and g=9.81 msg=$9.81\text{\,}\frac{\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{s}}$ is the gravitational acceleration.

Pedestrian Kinematics: The state of pedestrians is represented solely by the position:

𝐳a​(t)=𝐩a​(t).\mathbf{z}_{a}(t)=\mathbf{p}_{a}(t)\,. (12)

Since the motion patterns of pedestrians are generally more complex, we employ a first-order neural ordinary differential equation to model their kinematics. Their state evolves as:

𝐩˙a​(t)=fa​(𝐩a​(t),𝐮a​(t)),\dot{\mathbf{p}}_{a}(t)=f_{a}(\mathbf{p}_{a}(t),\mathbf{u}_{a}(t))\,, (13)

where faf_{a} is a neural network that parameterizes the state transition based on the control signal.

State Transitions: To integrate the kinematics, we employ Heun’s method. Let 𝐅a​(𝐳a​(t),𝐮a​(t))\mathbf{F}_{a}(\mathbf{z}_{a}(t),\mathbf{u}_{a}(t)) denote the time derivative of the state. First, an Euler prediction is computed:

𝐳aEuler​(t+Δ​t)=𝐳a​(t)+Δ​t​𝐅a​(𝐳a​(t),𝐮a​(t)).\mathbf{z}_{a}^{\text{Euler}}(t+\Delta t)=\mathbf{z}_{a}(t)+\Delta t\,\mathbf{F}_{a}(\mathbf{z}_{a}(t),\mathbf{u}_{a}(t))\,. (14)

Then, a correction update is applied:

𝐳a​(t+Δ​t)\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{a}(t+\Delta t) =𝐳a​(t)+Δ​t2​(𝐅a​(𝐳a​(t),𝐮a​(t))CLOSE\displaystyle=\mathbf{z}_{a}(t)+\frac{\Delta t}{2}(\mathbf{F}_{a}(\mathbf{z}_{a}(t),\mathbf{u}_{a}(t)) (15)
OPEN+𝐅a​(𝐳aEuler​(t+Δ​t),𝐮a​(t))).\displaystyle+\mathbf{F}_{a}(\mathbf{z}_{a}^{\text{Euler}}(t+\Delta t),\mathbf{u}_{a}(t)))\,.

By iteratively applying this integration for each future timestamp t=1,…,Tft=1,\dots,T_{f}, we extract the position components from 𝐳a​(t)\mathbf{z}_{a}(t) to form the candidate trajectories, denoted as Y~\tilde{Y}. They are then refined by the denoiser module to remove the diffusion noise and produce the final predictions.

III-E Denoising

The denoiser refines the candidate trajectories generated by the kinematic constraints. Given a candidate trajectory Y~\tilde{Y} obtained after kinematic refinement, Gaussian noise is first added according to a predefined diffusion schedule. The denoiser εθ\varepsilon_{\theta} then estimates this noise, conditioned on a context vector CC derived from the agent feature encoding, the dual map encoder, and the agent type embedding. The reverse diffusion update is given by:

Y^=1αβ​(Y~−1−αβ1−α¯β​εθ​(Y~,β,C))+σβ​z,\hat{Y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_{\beta}}}\left(\tilde{Y}-\frac{1-\alpha_{\beta}}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{\beta}}}\,\varepsilon_{\theta}(\tilde{Y},\beta,C)\right)+\sigma_{\beta}\,z, (16)

where αβ\alpha_{\beta}, α¯β\bar{\alpha}_{\beta}, and σβ\sigma_{\beta} are determined by the diffusion schedule and z∼𝒩⁡(0,I)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I). This procedure progressively removes the injected noise, yielding the final refined trajectory Y^\hat{Y}, which serves as one candidate output YakY_{a}^{k} for agent aa, forming part of the multi-modal prediction set 𝒴a\mathcal{Y}_{a}.

III-F Training

Our training procedure is divided into two stages. In the first stage, ground-truth future trajectories are perturbed with Gaussian noise according to a predefined diffusion schedule. The denoiser is pretrained to predict the injected noise by minimizing the mean squared error:

ℒdenoiser=‖ε−εθ​(Y~,β,C)‖2,\mathcal{L}_{\text{denoiser}}=\|\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{\theta}(\tilde{Y},\beta,C)\|^{2}\,, (17)

where ε\varepsilon is the added noise, Y~\tilde{Y} is the noisy trajectory obtained by perturbing the ground truth, β\beta is the diffusion timestamp, and CC is the conditioning context derived from the agent feature encoding, dual map encoder, and agent type embedding.

In the second stage, with the denoiser frozen, we train the encoding part (as shown in Fig. 2) using a weighted L2L_{2} reconstruction loss. We denote the ground-truth trajectory of an agent aa to be YaG​T∈ℝTf×2Y_{a}^{GT}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{f}\times 2}, and the KK candidate trajectories output by the denoiser as 𝒴a={Ya1,…,YaK}\mathcal{Y}_{a}=\{Y_{a}^{1},\dots,Y_{a}^{K}\}. The reconstruction loss is defined as:

ℒdiffuser=1|𝒜|​∑a∈𝒜mink∈{1,…,K}⁡‖Yak−YaG​T‖W2,\mathcal{L}_{\text{diffuser}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\min_{k\in\{1,\dots,K\}}\|Y_{a}^{k}-Y_{a}^{GT}\|_{W}^{2}\,, (18)

where ∥⋅∥W2\|\cdot\|_{W}^{2} denotes a weighted L2L_{2} norm. Additionally, the probability branch that yields candidate likelihoods for multi-modal prediction is supervised with a cross-entropy loss computed on the candidate probabilities. The loss targets are derived from the reconstruction errors, ensuring that the candidate with the lowest error is treated as the correct label.

IV Experiments

In this section, we first introduce the datasets and implementation details, then compare our proposed ParkDiffusion with several baselines, and finally present extensive ablation studies to analyze the impact of each component and evaluate the robustness of our approach.

IV-A Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate the performance of the model using standard trajectory prediction metrics. The minimum Average Displacement Error (minADE) calculates the Euclidean distance in meters between the ground-truth trajectory and the best of KK predicted trajectories as an average of all future time steps over all the agents. On the other hand, the minimum Final Displacement Error (minFDE) concerns the prediction error at the final time step, reflecting long-term performance. The Miss Rate (MR) is defined as the percentage of agents whose final prediction error exceeds 2.0 m2.0\text{\,}\mathrm{m}.

IV-B Setup and Implementation Details

We train our model on the Dragon Lake Parking (DLP) dataset [14] and the Intersections Drone (inD) dataset [15]. Both datasets are preprocessed into ego-vehicle centric data samples, consisting of all the vehicles and pedestrians within a 20 m20\text{\,}\mathrm{m} range around the ego vehicle. Our model predicts K=6K=6 multi-modal trajectories of all agents in the data samples for the next Tf=10T_{f}=10 timestamps, with a time interval of 0.4 s0.4\text{\,}\mathrm{s}. For comparison, we implement several trajectory prediction methods, including EKF, MultiPath++ [17], SceneTransformer [16], QCNet [7], and SIMPL [8]. We train all models using two NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs for 20 epochs to ensure convergence.

DLP Dataset: In the DLP dataset [14], we have agents of vehicle class (car, medium vehicle, bus) and pedestrian class. Since ParkPredict+ [14] employs a sequential network that first predicts agent intentions from Bird’s Eye View (BEV) images using a CNN and then feeds the features into a basic transformer, while ParkDiffusion uses polyline-based inputs, it is challenging to reproduce ParkPredict+ in our data preprocessing setting. Thus, we report the performance of the ParkPredict+ baseline based on their published results. For the other baselines, we integrate them into our data preprocessing pipeline and retrain them. Since the DLP dataset does not provide official data splits, we follow ParkPredict+, using 51,750 samples for training and 5,750 for validation.

inD Dataset: We also evaluate ParkDiffusion on the inD dataset by levelXdata [15]. Although it is not an automated parking dataset, it includes intersection scenarios featuring a mix of vehicles and vulnerable road users (VRUs), such as pedestrians, rendering it highly relevant to our research focus. The dataset consists of four traffic scenarios, from which we merge the “Bendplatz” and “Frankenburg” scenarios due to their high number of VRUs and then split the combined data into training and validation sets. After data preprocessing, we use 34,014 samples for training and 4,859 samples for validation.

IV-C Baseline Comparison

In this section, we compare ParkDiffusion with various baselines on the DLP and inD datasets.

DLP Dataset: We report the performance on the DLP dataset in Tab. I. We observe that ParkDiffusion substantially outperforms ParkPredict+, the only dedicated parking prediction baseline, as well as the driving prediction methods adapted to parking scenarios (EKF, MultiPath++, SceneTransformer, QCNet, and SIMPL). For vehicle trajectory prediction, ParkDiffusion achieves much lower minADE and minFDE scores compared to all other baselines. Most notably, our approach demonstrates strong performance in pedestrian prediction, with a significant margin of improvement relative to all other models, achieving a minADE of 0.15 m0.15\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, a minFDE of 0.32 m0.32\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, and an MR of 0.6 %0.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}. This enhanced accuracy is particularly critical in parking scenarios, where precise forecasting of pedestrian behavior is essential.

inD Dataset: In Tab. II, we report the results on the inD dataset. For vehicle trajectory prediction, SIMPL achieves the lowest minADE and MR, while ParkDiffusion obtains the best minFDE. In pedestrian prediction, ParkDiffusion demonstrates a clear advantage, achieving a minADE of 0.20 m0.20\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, a minFDE of 0.45 m0.45\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, and an MR of 1.8 %1.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}, compared to the minADE of MultiPath++ [17] (0.43 m0.43\text{\,}\mathrm{m}) and the minFDE and MR of SIMPL [8] (0.49 m0.49\text{\,}\mathrm{m}, 2.2 %2.2\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}). Overall, our method achieves the best minADE and minFDE scores compared to all baselines and matches SIMPL for the lowest MR in the combined evaluation. These results demonstrate that our approach achieves robust performance across diverse traffic settings, showing strong generalization and consistent accuracy in vehicle and pedestrian trajectory predictions.

IV-D Qualitative Results

Fig. 3 visualizes the prediction results of ParkDiffusion on both datasets. For the DLP dataset, our model accurately predicts the trajectories of vehicles and pedestrians, including turning and reverse maneuvers that are typically observed in automated parking scenarios. Moreover, the model maintains high prediction accuracy for pedestrians, even in environments crowded with multiple agents and complex interactions. In the inD dataset, we present multi-modal predictions for vehicles and pedestrians. These predictions effectively cover the ground-truth trajectory while capturing various possible movement patterns for different agents. The most challenging scenario is depicted in the bottom left figure, where a car is reversing in the intersection and switching to a new lane. Among the three candidate trajectories, one trajectory shows a slight deviation in the predicted direction while reflecting the vehicle’s speed. In contrast, the other two trajectories correctly capture the directional change but underestimate the speed. Overall, the general behavior of reversing and initiating movement in a different lane is captured well.

IV-E Ablation Studies

The ablation studies on the DLP dataset provide valuable insights into the impact of individual components and the robustness of our approach under varying conditions.

Components Analysis: In Tab. III, we present a detailed component-wise analysis of our approach. The baseline model is implemented by incorporating the Leapfrog diffusion approach [11] with our heterogeneous multi-agent multi-modal trajectory prediction pipeline. Subsequently, we integrate the dual map encoder, agent type embedding, and kinematic constraints module into the baseline model step by step. The results show that the map encoder substantially improves performance across the board. The agent type embeddings further refine the predictions, yielding a minor performance improvement. Finally, incorporating kinematic constraints further reduces prediction errors, achieving the best performance across all metrics.

Context Masking: In Tab. IV, we evaluate the impact of context masking on model performance. Starting with complete map information (0 %0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} masking), the model achieves the best results for vehicles and pedestrians. As the amount of masking increases, thus limiting the available contextual data, the performance gradually degrades. Notably, while 25 %25\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} masking results in only minor performance reductions, more extensive masking (50 %50\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} to 100 %100\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}) leads to a marked increase in prediction errors. These results indicate that model performance deteriorates with the loss of contextual information, underscoring the importance of accurate map context to achieve reliable trajectory prediction.

Number of Agents: Finally, in Tab. V, we study how the number of agents in a scene influences the performance of our proposed model. For this experiment, we categorized scenes according to their number of agents to analyze how an increase in agent density impacts the prediction accuracy. The results reveal that vehicle trajectory performance degrades as the number of agents increases, while pedestrian predictions tend to improve in denser scenes, potentially benefiting from richer interaction cues. Overall, although vehicle errors increase with higher agent counts, the improvements in pedestrian predictions lead to minor variations in the aggregated performance metrics across all agents.

V Conclusion

In this paper, we introduced ParkDiffusion, a novel diffusion-based framework for heterogeneous multi-agent trajectory prediction in automated parking scenarios. Our approach leverages several key components, including an agent encoder, a dual map encoder, an agent type embedding, and a kinematic refinement module. The overall goal of the approach is to capture complex environmental contexts and accurately forecast trajectories for both vehicles and pedestrians. Notably, ParkDiffusion demonstrates superior performance in pedestrian trajectory prediction, which is especially critical in traffic environments with a high prevalence of vulnerable road users. Extensive experiments, including baseline comparisons on two datasets and various ablation studies, validate the accuracy and robustness of our approach. In future work, we will investigate an extension of our model to additional agent types to further enhance the modeling of heterogeneous interactions.
